{{Short description|1951 song by Tom Lehrer}}
{{CS1 config|mode=cs2}}
{{Listen|type=music|filename=1-06 Lobachevsky.mp3|title=Lobachevsky|description=Lehrer sings "Lobachevsky"}}
"'''Lobachevsky'''" is a humorous song by [[Tom Lehrer]], referring to the mathematician [[Nikolai Lobachevsky|Nikolai Ivanovich Lobachevsky]].<ref>{{citation |url=http://dmdb.org/lyrics/lehrer.revisited.html#6 |title=Lobachevsky |publisher=The Demented Music Database |accessdate=2 October 2014}}</ref>
According to Lehrer, the song is "not intended as a slur on [Lobachevsky's] character" and the name was chosen "solely for [[prosodic]] reasons".<ref>Liner notes, "The Tom Lehrer Collection", ''Shout!'' Factory, 2010</ref><ref name="bessman"/>

In the introduction, Lehrer describes the song as an adaptation of a routine that [[Danny Kaye]] did to honor the Russian actor [[Constantin Stanislavski]].<ref name="bessman"/> (The Danny Kaye routine is sung from the perspective of a famous Russian actor who learns and applies Stanislavski's secret to [[method acting]]: "Suffer.") <ref> [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jXI2djKeerQ The Stanislavski routine] performed on the Danny Kaye Radio Show </ref> Lehrer sings the song from the point of view of an eminent Russian mathematician who learns from Lobachevsky that [[plagiarism]] is the secret of success in mathematics ("only be sure always to call it please '[[research]]{{'"}}). The narrator later uses this strategy to get a paper published ahead of a rival, then to write a book and earn a fortune selling the movie rights.

Lehrer wrote that he did not know [[Russian language|Russian]]. In the song he quotes two "book reviews" in Russian; the first is a long sentence that he then translates succinctly as "It stinks." The second, a different but equally long sentence, is also translated as "It stinks." The actual text of these sentences bear no relation to academics: the first phrase quotes [[Modest Mussorgsky|Mussorgsky]]'s "[[The Song of the Flea|Song of the Flea]]": {{langx|ru|Жил-был король когда-то, при нём блоха жила|Zhil-byl korol' kogda-to, pri nom blokha zhila|Once there was a king who had a pet flea}}. The second references a Russian joke: {{langx|ru|Я иду туда, куда сам царь идёт пешком|Ya idu tuda, kuda sam tsar' idot peshkom|Now I must go where even the Tsar goes on foot}} [the bathroom].<ref name="lobachevsky.htm">{{citation |title="Lobachevsky" Words and music by Tom Lehrer |url=http://www.haverford.edu/physics/songs/lehrer/lobachevsky.htm |publisher=PhysicsSongs.org |accessdate=October 2, 2014}}</ref>

At 115 seconds in, the song briefly quotes [[Hungarian Rhapsody No. 2]] by [[Franz Liszt]].

The song was first performed as part of ''The Physical Revue,'' a 1951–1952 musical [[revue]] by Lehrer and a few other professors.<ref>{{citation |title=The Physical Revue, by Tom Lehrer |url=http://www.haverford.edu/astronomy/songs/lehrer/physrev.htm |publisher=PhysicsSongs.org |accessdate=October 2, 2014}}</ref> It is track 6 on ''[[Songs by Tom Lehrer]]'', which was re-released as part of ''[[Songs & More Songs by Tom Lehrer]]'' and ''[[The Remains of Tom Lehrer]]''. In this early version, [[Ingrid Bergman]] is named to star in the role of "the [[Hypotenuse]]" in ''The Eternal Triangle'', a film purportedly based on the narrator's book.<ref name="Calder2005">{{citation|author=Nigel Calder|title=Magic Universe: A Grand Tour of Modern Science|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=E4NfZ9FDcc8C&pg=PT639 |year=2005 |publisher=[[Oxford University Press]] |isbn=978-0-19-162235-9|page=639}}</ref> It was recorded again for ''[[Revisited (Tom Lehrer album)]]'', with [[Brigitte Bardot]] as the Hypotenuse. A third recording is included in ''[[Tom Lehrer Discovers Australia (And Vice Versa)]]'', a live album recorded in Australia, featuring [[Marilyn Monroe]] as the Hypotenuse. A fourth recording was made in 1966 when ''Songs by Tom Lehrer'' was reissued in stereo, with [[Doris Day]] playing the Hypotenuse.<ref>{{citation |url=http://dmdb.org/lyrics/lehrer.diff.html |title=Tom Lehrer lyric variations |date=April 2, 1995 |publisher=The Demented Music Database |accessdate=2 October 2014}}</ref><ref name="lobachevsky.htm"/>

In 1957, while working for the [[National Security Agency]], Lehrer coauthored a paper in which he snuck in the song's line "Analytic and Algebraic Topology of Locally Euclidean Metrizations of Infinitely Differentiable Riemannian Manifolds" into the reference section as an uncited and unpublished paper by Lobachevsky.<ref>{{citation |last1=Fagen |first1=R. E |last2=Lehrer |first2=T. A. |title=The gambler's ruin with soft hearted adversary |url=https://media.defense.gov/2021/Jul/14/2002762807/-1/-1/0/GAMBLERS-RUIN.PDF/GAMBLERS-RUIN.PDF |publisher=[[National Security Agency]] |date=24 January 1957 |quote=Reference 3: Lobachevsky "Analytic and Algebraic Topology of Locally Euclidean Metrizations of Infinitely Differentiable Riemannian Manifolds" (Unpublished)}}</ref> 

The song is frequently quoted,<ref>{{citation|title=Concise Oxford Dictionary of Quotations|editor-first=Susan|editor-last=Ratcliffe|publisher=Oxford University Press|year=2006|isbn=9780198614173|page=692|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=zLDEH2TAvwUC&pg=PT692}}. See also the ''Oxford Dictionary of Quotations'' (1999), [https://books.google.com/books?id=o6rFno1ffQoC&pg=PA462 p.&nbsp;462], and the ''Oxford Dictionary of Modern Quotations'' (2007), [https://books.google.com/books?id=rjLTsncFKCgC&pg=PA195 p.&nbsp;195].</ref><ref>{{citation|title=Mathematical quotations for all occasions|first=Barbara|last=Curcic|journal=The Mathematics Teacher|volume=69|issue=1|date=January 1976|pages=40–44|doi=10.5951/MT.69.1.0040|jstor=27960358}}.</ref><ref>{{citation|title=The Yale Book of Quotations|editor-first=Fred R.|editor-last=Shapiro|publisher=Yale University Press|year=2006|isbn=9780300107982|page=450|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ck6bXqt5shkC&pg=PA450}}.</ref> especially in works about plagiarism.<ref>{{citation | last = Berlin | first = Leonard | date = October 2008 | doi = 10.1007/s00256-008-0599-0 | issue = 1 | journal = Skeletal Radiology | pages = 1–4 | title = Plagiarism, salami slicing, and Lobachevsky | volume = 38| pmid = 18828008 | s2cid = 29316983 | doi-access = free }}.</ref><ref>{{citation|title=Research in Medical and Biological Sciences: From Planning and Preparation to Grant Application and Publication|first1=Petter|last1=Laake|first2=Haakon Breien|last2=Benestad|author2-link=Haakon Breien Benestad|publisher=Academic Press|year=2015|isbn=9780128001547|page=55|contribution-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=p9icBAAAQBAJ&pg=PA55|contribution=2.5.2 Plagiarism}}.</ref><ref>{{citation|title=The Writer's Book of Wisdom: 101 Rules for Mastering Your Craft|first=Steven|last=Goldsberry|publisher=Writer's Digest Books|year=2007|isbn=9781582974941|page=23|contribution-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=GBkVnrzMc4gC&pg=PA23|contribution=Borrow (and steal) from your favorite writers}}.</ref> Writing about it in ''[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]'', [[Jim Bessman]] calls the song "dazzlingly inventive in its shameless promotion of plagiarism", calling out in particular a sequence in which Lehrer strings together rhymes from the names of ten {{sic|Russian|expected=formerly all were USSR cities but now are in multiple nations}} cities.<ref name="bessman">{{citation|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=jRAEAAAAMBAJ&pg=PA53 |title=Words & Music|first=Jim|last=Bessman|magazine=[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]|date=March 30, 2002|page=53|volume=114|issue=13}}.</ref>
Mathematician [[Jordan Ellenberg]] has called it "surely the greatest comic musical number of all time about mathematical publishing".<ref>{{citation|title=How Not to Be Wrong: The Power of Mathematical Thinking|first=Jordan|last=Ellenberg|authorlink=Jordan Ellenberg|publisher=Penguin|year=2014|isbn=9780698163843|page=396|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=2k9KAgAAQBAJ&pg=PA396}}.</ref>
